p: 3.1 Problem formulation. Given a query q and an intent space \mathcal{I} (from public datasets), the system outputs a primary intent \hat{y}\in\mathcal{I}, an ordered set of secondary intents \hat{S}=\{\hat{y}_2,\dots,\hat{y}_K\}, and an uncertainty u. A three-state decision applies thresholds (\tau_{lo},\tau_{hi}): release if u\ge\tau_{hi}; clarify (return the candidate intent set for user confirmation) if \tau_{lo}\le u<\tau_{hi}; refuse (route to human / safe fallback) if u<\tau_{lo}. Unlike single-label ambiguity tasks, the ground truth here is itself a variable-length intent set Y (a query may satisfy multiple intents simultaneously); thus the object of coverage is not a fixed label but the set similarity between Y and the predicted set \hat{S} (Jaccard / symmetric difference). Under the training-free setting there is no classifier emitting logits; uncertainty is constructed from retrieval evidence and LLM self-assessment.

3.2 Module 1: Intent knowledge base and retrieval-augmented reasoning. The knowledge base is built from the training splits of public datasets with zero annotation: intent definitions plus example utterances. The index contains intent-level prototypes and utterance-level vectors. Retrieval returns the top-K_r candidate intents (hyperparameter) as evidence context for the LLM, which outputs the primary intent plus the ordered secondary-intent set. Both K and K_r are ablated (Section 4.5).

3.3 Module 2 (Contribution A): retrieval-grounded, classifier-free set-valued conformal calibration. Existing conformal intent methods (e.g., CICC [31]) assume a trained classifier that emits scores; the training-free route only has retrieval similarities and LLM self-reported confidence, both unreliable and correlated. We construct a fused nonconformity score s(q)=g(\text{retrieval statistics [top-}K_r\text{ similarity, top1-top2 margin, distance to confirmed entries]}, \text{LLM self-assessment}), and apply split conformal on a calibration set. The risk measure is the Jaccard similarity between the predicted set \hat{S} and the true set Y, controlling the set-level error rate (probability that the symmetric difference exceeds a threshold) within 1-\alpha. This extends conformal prediction from single-point coverage to variable-length multi-intent set coverage, without any gradient training.

3.4 Module 3 (Contribution B): adaptive minimal clarification set. Clarification no longer returns a fixed K candidates; instead, under the conformal guarantee of Module 2 it returns the minimal set that covers the true intent set Y with probability \ge 1-\alpha. Ambiguous / long-tail queries return 2–3 candidates, clear queries return 1, and out-of-scope queries return 0 (direct refusal). The three-state thresholds (\tau_{lo},\tau_{hi}) are calibrated on the validation set to maximize refusal recall under an FPR95 constraint; refusal preserves the safe-fallback semantics. The three modules are independently ablatable, corresponding to Section 4.5. The overall framework is shown in Figure 1 (design doc): knowledge-base construction and retrieval are decoupled from reasoning—zero-annotation KB construction, training-free retrieval and LLM reasoning, with light fine-tuning (LoRA/SetFit) as control only. The key differences from CICC (single-label, trained classifier, TODS scenario) lie in Modules 2/3: classifier-free scores, variable-length multi-intent sets, and Web single-turn refusal.

4.1 Setup. We evaluate on CLINC150 (150 in-scope intents, native OOS, ~5.5k test queries), MixATIS (~828 test queries, 1–3 intents), and MixSNIPS (~2,199 test queries, 1–3 intents), all public and unchanged. All methods are evaluated under a unified protocol v1.0: \alpha=0.1 split conformal; empty sets (refusal) counted in the full denominator; macro-F1 from sklearn macro (zero-division 0); ECE in 15 bins on the primary-intent top-1 confidence (Ours = 1 minus the minimal fused score); false-refusal rate = fraction of in-domain queries predicted as empty; OOS metrics on CLINC150 only; Hit@k over all true intents; the release / clarify / reject states are mutually exclusive. Two independent runs (seed42 / seed123) are averaged. Baselines: R10 UniCR [34], R5 CICC [31], R12 MULACONF [33], R12-QP QP-OneModel [12] (recomputed under v1.0, 3 seeds), R11 TECP-style token-entropy [35] (qwen3-8b/14b), R13 SetFit+MC-Dropout hybrid routing, and few-shot LLM baselines (Qwen3-8B/14B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill, 3/5/10-shot; appendix A).

4.2 Main results. Table T2a (CLINC150): Ours reaches F1 0.899 / IoU 0.856 / coverage(J≥0.5) 0.856 / avg set 0.87 / ECE 0.005 / false-refusal 0.139 / OOS refusal 1.000 / AUROC 0.978. It is the only method with 100% OOS refusal and near-perfect calibration, while staying within 0.6pt F1 of the strongest conformal baseline (R10, F1 0.905). Table T2b (MixATIS / MixSNIPS): Ours achieves IoU 0.387 / 0.757, Hit@3 0.239 / 0.619, avg set 1.52 / 1.80, ECE 0.219 / 0.045, clarify rates 0.728 / 0.839. Against multi-intent set baselines: MULACONF's sets are unusable on multi-intent data (avg set 150.6–748.5, false-refusal up to 1.0); QP-OneModel v1.0 remains below Ours even at 10-shot (IoU 0.299 / 0.460 vs. 0.387 / 0.757) while refusing nothing and triggering clarify on 97% of MixATIS queries (statistical trigger, not a risk decision); R11 TECP-style achieves comparable MixATIS IoU (0.368/0.384) but with ECE 0.471–0.566 and 5× LLM calls; R13 trades API cost (6.3–15.9% LLM call rate) but its set quality (IoU 0.190/0.302/0.475) and calibration (ECE 0.374–0.695) are far below Ours, with only 5.7% OOS refusal on CLINC150. Few-shot LLM baselines (Qwen3-14B 10-shot) lead in raw F1/IoU (0.956; 0.872 / 0.952) but provide no coverage guarantee, no OOS refusal, and no clarification interaction; their ECE is not computable under v1.0.

4.3 Risk-controlled comparison (P0). P0-1 (equal-risk operating point, zero API): tightening the OOS gate from FPR 0.05 to 0.0005 raises Ours F1 0.899→0.929 and reduces false refusal 0.139→0.097 while keeping OOS refusal at 1.000 and ECE≤0.008—an equal-risk curve (Figure F11) shows Ours dominates QP and LLM few-shot in the calibrated region. P0-2 (clarify-fair oracle): under oracle clarification, Ours MixSNIPS IoU 0.754→0.942 (vs. 0.952 few-shot) and MixATIS 0.396→0.760 (vs. 0.872): the multi-intent gap is largely a reporting-convention difference, and Ours keeps tighter avg sets (1.52/1.80 vs. 2.15/2.01) for interaction control.

4.4 Efficiency and system-level comparison (R13). R13 (SetFit + MC-Dropout routing, LLM fallback) is the industrial hybrid-routing baseline. It saves API cost (6.3–15.9% LLM call rate) but has no coverage guarantee and weak set ability (Section 4.2). Compared with Ours, the training-free route needs no labels, no GPU fine-tuning, and supports instant knowledge updates (A8, drift-before/after coverage gap remains controlled), at the cost of ~1.6–2.7% F1 vs. light fine-tuning controls (P3).

4.5 Ablations (P3). (A1) K ablation (k_max∈{0,1,2,3}): K=1 is optimal for compactness/coverage trade-off. (A3) fusion alpha {0.0,1.0}: rank-normalized fusion with α=0.1 (retrieval-dominant with LLM auxiliary) is stable; pure retrieval (0.0) or pure LLM (1.0) both degrade calibration. (A5) K_r retrieval candidates {1,3,5}: K_r=1 suffices; more candidates add noise. (A9) cross-domain generalization: CLINC150-calibrated Ours transfers to MixSNIPS test with controlled coverage loss. (A4) set-level risk metric, (A2) temperature scaling comparison, (A8) knowledge-update simulation: all confirm the design choices. Main hyperparameters: K=1, K_r=1, fa=0.1, τ_aux=0.5. Light fine-tuning (LoRA) and KB example-count ablations are deferred (W4).

We presented a training-free, retrieval-grounded framework that unifies single-turn multi-intent set output with calibrated three-state refusal. On three public benchmarks, it is the only method combining finite-sample coverage guarantees, 100% OOS refusal, strong calibration, and tight sets, at zero training cost; its F1 gap to few-shot LLM baselines narrows to ~2.7pt under an equal-risk operating point. Limitations: MixATIS remains challenging (IoU 0.387, ECE 0.219); the LLM back-bone's self-assessment is still a proxy for logits; and web-scale long-tail generalization beyond public benchmarks is untested. Future work includes light-fine-tuning gains (LoRA/SetFit, W4), scaling to open-web queries (Needle in the Web / VibeSearchBench), and extending stratified set-valued conformal to multi-turn clarification with memory.
